root-locus.title: Root Locus
root-locus.intro: The root locus shows how the closed-loop poles of a feedback system migrate across the complex plane as a single loop gain $K$ is swept from zero to a large value. It turns a stability question into a geometric one.
root-locus.purpose: This tool plots the locus of the roots of $1 + K\,G(s)H(s) = 0$ for the transfer function you enter, draws the asymptotes, breakaway points and imaginary-axis crossings, and marks the closed-loop poles that correspond to the current gain. A second plot shows the closed-loop step response for that same $K$, so you can watch pole position turn into damping, overshoot and speed.

model.heading: Characteristic equation and the two criteria
model.body: With the open-loop transfer function written as $G(s)H(s) = N(s)/D(s)$, the closed-loop poles are the roots of $D(s) + K\,N(s) = 0$. A point $s$ lies on the locus if and only if it satisfies both the angle criterion and the magnitude criterion. The angle criterion, $\sum \theta_{zeros} - \sum \theta_{poles} = (2k+1)180^\circ$, selects the geometry of the branches and does not depend on $K$. The magnitude criterion, $|K\,G(s)H(s)| = 1$, then assigns a unique gain $K$ to every point of a branch.

model.heading: Branches, endpoints and asymptotes
model.body: For $n$ open-loop poles and $m$ zeros, the locus has $n$ branches. Each branch starts at a pole when $K = 0$ and ends at a zero, or at infinity, when $K \to \infty$. The $n - m$ branches that escape follow asymptotes with real-axis centroid $\sigma_a = (\sum p_i - \sum z_i)/(n - m)$ and angles $\theta_a = (2k+1)\pi/(n - m)$. On the real axis, a segment belongs to the locus when the total number of real poles and zeros to its right is odd.

model.heading: Breakaway and break-in points
model.body: Where two branches meet on the real axis and leave it, the gain $K(s) = -D(s)/N(s)$ passes through an extremum along the axis. Solving $dK/ds = 0$ gives candidate points, and only those whose gain $K$ is real and positive and which lie on a valid real-axis segment are true breakaway (leaving) or break-in (entering) points.

model.heading: Imaginary-axis crossings and stability
model.body: The gain at which the locus enters the right half-plane follows from the Routh-Hurwitz array of $D(s) + K\,N(s)$. Setting the first-column entry of the $s^1$ row to zero gives the critical gain $K_{cr}$. The auxiliary polynomial of the preceding row, evaluated at that gain, gives the crossing frequency $\omega_{cr}$. For gains below $K_{cr}$ all poles stay in the left half-plane and the loop is stable.

equations: Closed-loop characteristic equation whose roots form the locus.
Angle criterion: decides whether a test point belongs to the locus.
Magnitude criterion: gives the gain at a point on the locus.
Asymptote centroid on the real axis.

Moves the closed-loop poles along the branches. The slider range is bounded by the editable limits $K_{min}$ and $K_{max}$, which default to $0.01$ and $10$.

Shows the branches, the asymptotes with their centroid $\sigma_a$, and the current closed-loop poles. The grid can be switched between Cartesian and polar so that lines of constant $\zeta$ and $\omega_n$ are visible.

applications.body: Choosing the proportional gain of a joint position loop so that the dominant poles stay well damped and away from the imaginary axis.
Studying how an autopilot gain moves the short-period and phugoid poles as the gain changes.

Setting automatic voltage regulator gain so that generator excitation control stays stable across operating points.

pid.title: PID Controller
pid.intro: A PID controller combines proportional, integral and derivative action on the error signal. It remains the most widely deployed feedback law in industrial automation because each term has a clear physical meaning.
pid.purpose: This tool closes a feedback loop around the plant transfer function you enter, using a P, I, D, PI, PD or PID controller in one of several forms. It simulates the response to the selected reference signal and reports overshoot, peak time, settling time and steady-state error, so you can see directly what each gain does.

model.heading: Parallel and ISA standard forms
model.body: In the parallel form the control signal is $u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e(\tau)d\tau + K_d\,de(t)/dt$ with independent gains. The standard ISA form factors out the proportional gain, $C(s) = K_p\left(1 + 1/(T_i s) + T_d s/\left((T_d/N)s + 1\right)\right)$, so that $T_i$ and $T_d$ are times. The two forms are equivalent when $K_i = K_p/T_i$ and $K_d = K_p T_d$.

model.heading: Derivative filter
model.body: A pure derivative is not realisable and amplifies measurement noise. In this tool the filter is applied only by the modified subtypes (Parallel Modified and Series Modified), where the derivative term is $K_d s/(1 + s/N)$: the filter pole sits at $s = -N$ and the high-frequency derivative gain is $K_d N$. The textbook ISA form, $C(s) = K_p(1 + 1/(T_i s) + T_d s/((T_d/N)s + 1))$, has its filter pole at $s = -N/T_d$ and high-frequency gain $K_p(1 + N)$; it is the reference form, not a setting of this tool. The default subtype, Parallel Standard, has no filter, so $N$ has no effect on it. Typical values of $N$ lie between $5$ and $20$, and a larger $N$ gives a faster derivative at the price of more noise.

model.heading: Integrator anti-windup
model.body: Background, not simulated by this tool: the simulator is linear and has no actuator saturation, so the clamp below is never active in any scope shown here. In a real controller, when the actuator saturates, the integral state keeps growing and later causes a long overshoot. Clamping freezes the integrator whenever the unsaturated command $v$ lies outside $[u_{min}, u_{max}]$ and the error has the same sign as $v$. The integrator resumes as soon as the error drives the command back into range.

model.heading: Transient metrics
model.body: For a dominant second-order closed loop with damping ratio $\zeta$ and natural frequency $\omega_n$, the percent overshoot is $M_p = e^{-\pi\zeta/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}} \times 100\%$ and the two percent settling time is $t_s \approx 4/(\zeta\omega_n)$. The rise time is approximated by $t_r \approx (\pi - \arccos\zeta)/(\omega_n\sqrt{1-\zeta^2})$. Raising $K_p$ shortens $t_r$, adding $K_i$ removes steady-state error to a step, and adding $K_d$ increases damping.

equations: Parallel PID control law in the time domain.

applications.body: Speed and current loops of servo drives, where anti-windup protects against voltage and current limits during acceleration.

Attitude and altitude hold loops that use gain scheduling around PID controllers across the flight envelope.
Inverter and converter regulators, as well as turbine speed governors, tuned for a specified overshoot and settling time.

frequency-response.title: Frequency Response
frequency-response.intro: Frequency response describes how a linear system scales and shifts sinusoids of every frequency. From the open-loop response alone, stability margins of the closed loop can be read without solving for any pole.
frequency-response.purpose: This tool evaluates $G(j\omega)$ for the transfer function you enter and displays it as a Bode plot, a Nyquist plot or a Nichols chart. It marks the gain and phase crossover frequencies, reports the gain and phase margins, decomposes the response into first-order and second-order factors, and correlates the margins with the closed-loop step response.

model.heading: Magnitude and phase
model.body: Setting $s = j\omega$ gives a complex number whose magnitude in decibels is $|G(j\omega)|_{dB} = 20\log_{10}|G(j\omega)|$ and whose phase is $\angle G(j\omega)$. For a product of factors, the decibel magnitudes and the phases simply add, which is why asymptotic Bode sketches are built from straight-line segments. Each simple pole bends the magnitude slope by $-20\text{ dB/decade}$ and the phase by $-90^\circ$, and each simple zero does the opposite.

model.heading: Crossover frequencies
model.body: The gain crossover frequency $\omega_{gc}$ is where the magnitude crosses unity, so $|G(j\omega_{gc})| = 1$, which is $0\text{ dB}$. The phase crossover frequency $\omega_{pc}$ is where the phase equals $-180^\circ$, so $\angle G(j\omega_{pc}) = -180^\circ$. These two points anchor every stability margin.

model.heading: Gain margin and phase margin
model.body: The gain margin is the extra loop gain that brings the system to the edge of instability, $GM = -20\log_{10}|G(j\omega_{pc})|\text{ dB}$. The phase margin is the extra phase lag tolerated at the gain crossover, $PM = 180^\circ + \angle G(j\omega_{gc})$. For a stable minimum-phase loop both must be positive. A phase margin near $60^\circ$ typically gives a well damped step response.

model.heading: Closed-loop bandwidth
model.body: With $T(s) = G(s)/(1 + G(s))$, the closed-loop bandwidth $\omega_b$ is the frequency at which $|T(j\omega)|$ falls to $1/\sqrt{2}$ of its low-frequency value, that is $-3\text{ dB}$. Bandwidth indicates how quickly the loop can follow commands, and it is close to $\omega_{gc}$ for loops with a moderate phase margin.

state-space.title: State Space
state-space.intro: State-space modelling describes a dynamic system through first-order differential equations in a vector of internal states. It handles multi-input multi-output systems naturally and underlies modern control design.
state-space.purpose: This tool lets you edit the matrices $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$ and $D$ of a second-order or third-order system and computes the characteristic polynomial, the open-loop eigenvalues, the controllability and observability matrices with their ranks, and a state-feedback gain that places the closed-loop poles where you request. Phase portraits show the resulting state trajectories.

model.heading: State and output equations
model.body: The model is $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{B}u$ and $y = \mathbf{C}\mathbf{x} + D u$, where $\mathbf{x}$ has $n$ components. The transfer function is $G(s) = \mathbf{C}(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{B} + D$, and its poles are the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$, found from the characteristic equation $\det(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}) = 0$.

model.heading: State transition matrix
model.body: With $u = 0$ the solution is $\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{\Phi}(t)\mathbf{x}(0)$ with $\mathbf{\Phi}(t) = e^{\mathbf{A}t}$. It equals the inverse Laplace transform of $(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})^{-1}$. The system is asymptotically stable when every eigenvalue of $\mathbf{A}$ has a negative real part.

model.heading: Controllability and observability
model.body: The pair $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B})$ is controllable when the matrix $\mathcal{C}$ has rank $n$, meaning the input can steer the state anywhere. The pair $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{C})$ is observable when $\mathcal{O}$ has rank $n$, meaning the state can be reconstructed from the output. A rank deficiency reveals a mode that the input cannot move or the output cannot see.

model.heading: Pole placement and Ackermann's formula
model.body: With full-state feedback $u = -\mathbf{K}\mathbf{x}$ the closed-loop matrix is $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}\mathbf{K}$. If the system is controllable, any set of desired poles $\lambda_i^{d}$ can be assigned. For a single input, Ackermann's formula gives $\mathbf{K} = [0\ \cdots\ 0\ 1]\,\mathcal{C}^{-1}\varphi(\mathbf{A})$, where $\varphi$ is the desired characteristic polynomial evaluated at the matrix $\mathbf{A}$.

applications.body: Full-state feedback for aircraft and spacecraft attitude control with several coupled axes.
Balancing robots and inverted pendulums, where the state holds angle, angular rate, position and velocity.
Multivariable control of microgrids and converters, with observers estimating unmeasured currents.
Multi-axis motion platforms, where controllability analysis shows whether every axis can be commanded independently.
Active suspension and lane keeping, using observability to decide which sensors are needed.
